1.pericope_label: Jezebel threatens Elijah, who flees to Beersheba and is fed by the angel on his way to Horeb

schools.summary: Henry reads Ahab’s report as deliberate provocation rather than confession: his conscience retained too much of the Israelite to let him persecute Elijah himself, so he told his wife not what God had done but what Elijah had done, as though the man had fetched fire from heaven by a spell, and he called the slain priests simply the prophets, as if none but they deserved the name, never noticing that their death was reprisal for her killing of God’s own prophets. On the oath he observes that it proves only that she meant Elijah to believe she would kill him, and remarks that the gods she swore by could do her no harm. He refuses to excuse the flight at all — shall we praise him for this? we praise him not — since he who stood undaunted amid the terrors of heaven and earth trembles at the menaces of a proud passionate woman.

Clarke contradicts Henry in six words, judging that Ahab told Jezebel probably with no evil design against Elijah. He accounts for the collapse by frustrated expectation, Elijah having thought the miracle at Carmel would convert the whole court and country and finding himself mistaken; he reads the southern frontier as a place of safety under Judah’s jurisdiction, and the servant left behind either because one man alone was less likely to be discovered or because Elijah did not wish to risk his life. On the forty days he notes only that the fast matched Moses’s at the same mountain and our Lord’s in the wilderness.

Gill holds that Jezebel sent her message only to frighten him away, not daring to seize him for fear of the people, and finds a hand of Providence in the delay that gave him time to escape. He turns the contrast of courage into doctrine: that one who had faced four hundred and fifty priests should be terrified at a single woman’s threats shows the spirit and courage he had before were of the Lord and not of himself, since those of the greatest zeal, left to themselves, grow weak and timorous. On the provision he follows Bochart in rendering the cake as baked on hot stones after the eastern manner.

Keil and Delitzsch call the threat the impotence of a woman’s rage, already detected by the early commentators: she wanted only to be rid of him, unable to put him to death partly on account of the people, who were enthusiastic in his favour, and partly on account of the king, upon whom the affair at Carmel had not been without salutary effect. They take the note that Beersheba belonged to Judah as showing he meant to leave the kingdom of Israel altogether, the scene of his labours, as Jeremiah in a like inward conflict wished he might leave his people; they describe the bread cake baked over red-hot stones, still a favourite with the Bedouins; and from the journey they draw the inference that since the angel never told him where to go, yet he walked to Horeb, it must have been his intention from the first to go into the desert and see whether the Lord would still acknowledge him, reading in the strength imparted an indication to follow the footsteps of divine grace farther in and make a pilgrimage to the mountain where God had revealed his counsel to Moses. Ellicott reads the despondency as temperament, the sudden reaction being eminently characteristic of an impulsive and vehement nature whose blow had been struck as it thought triumphantly and which now feels a cool unrelenting antagonism unshaken and only embittered by all that had passed; he finds the note about Judah significant the other way, that kingdom being then in half-dependent alliance with Israel, so that even under Jehoshaphat Elijah might not be safe there though his servant could stay without danger. On the words under the tree he reads a collapsed hope: the exclamation is characteristic, for evidently Elijah had hoped that he himself was better than his fathers, singled out beyond all who went before to be the victorious champion of a great crisis, he and he alone, and now he thinks that hope vain and asks why he should live when the rest of the prophets have died. He doubts the forty days were spent walking, the distance being some two hundred miles, and takes them for an interval of retirement and solitary meditation in which the prophet’s spirit might be calmed from its alternations of triumph and despondency; and he observes how rarely angels appear during the prophetic period, as though the place of their spiritual ministry had been supplied by the prophetic mission itself, so that here the angel is but auxiliary to the prophet, as the angel of the Agony to the Prophet of prophets.

9.pericope_label: Elijah in the cave at Horeb: what doest thou here, the wind, earthquake and fire, and the still small voice

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch deny that the question involves a reproof, as though Elijah had nothing to do there, holding it simply intended to lead him to utter the thoughts and feelings of his heart; they take the definite article as pointing back to the cleft of the rock in which Moses stood while the glory of Jehovah passed by. In the complaint they find not only the greatest despair but a carnal zeal that would gladly have called down the immediate vengeance of the Almighty upon all idolaters, and a tacit reproof that God had looked on so long at the conduct of the ungodly. They read the whole theophany as a repetition of the appearance granted to Moses on Sinai, tempest, earthquake and fire being signs of the Lord’s coming to judgment and more terrible still in the awful solitude of the Horeb mountains, while the gentle rustling revealed him as merciful and gracious, long-suffering and of great goodness and truth — and the answer that followed showed that he does not leave guilt unpunished. Ellicott suggests the message came in vision or dream at night, the Greek inserting the word to-morrow, so that what Elijah replies in imagination he repeats next day in actual words; he offers the alternative that the article is anticipatory, naming not a cave already famous but the one Elijah’s sojourn was to make so. He calls the complaint impatient self-exculpation and even remonstrance — Elijah had been jealous for the Lord, yet the Lord had not been jealous for himself — and sets it beside Isaiah’s cry that God would rend the heavens, Jonah’s anger, and the message sent from prison to our Lord, finding in the Elias of the New Testament the same despondent impatience. On the vision he reads the two earlier Horeb manifestations against each other: to the people, power made visible, because the whirlwind, earthquake and fire were the natural clothing of the terrors of the Law and perhaps the only signs for which their hearts were then prepared; to Moses, not the divine majesty but the Name, the Lord God merciful and gracious. Elijah’s vision contrasts with the first and harmonises with the second, disclaiming the manifestation in power and vengeance for which he had by implication craved and implying in the voice of a light breath the higher power of the Spirit, which the terrors of external power cannot reach — not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit.

Henry hears the question reproving twice over, for the fleeing and for the fixing. Laying the emphasis on the pronoun, he asks whether so great a prophet, so famed for resolution, should forsake his colours, a cowardice more excusable in another and not so bad an example: should such a man as I flee? Howl, fir-trees, if the cedars be thus shaken. Then he asks whether a cave is a place for a prophet of the Lord to lodge in, and whether this is a time for such men to retreat when the public has such need of them, noting that in his earlier retirement Elijah had at least been a blessing to a widow at Sarepta while here he had no opportunity of doing good. He defends the complaint itself, asking that the retreat be imputed not to want of zeal but to despair of success, since while there was hope of doing good he had been very jealous for the Lord and now had laboured in vain; yet he grants that the apostle calls this making intercession against Israel, the advocate necessitated at last to be his people’s accuser. On the charge that the altars were thrown down he explains that these were the private altars the prophets of the Lord kept, attended by good people who could not go up to Jerusalem and would not worship the calves or Baal, and that though such separate altars broke in upon the unity of the church, being erected and attended by those who sincerely aimed at God’s glory the seeming schism was excused, for God owned them as his own. He notices the reversal in the manner of the appearance, that Moses was put into the cave when the glory passed while Elijah was called out of it, and draws the lesson from what moved him: the wind and earthquake and fire did not make him cover his face, but the still voice did, gracious souls being more affected by the tender mercies of the Lord than by his terrors.

Gill reports that the cave is shown to travellers to this day at the foot of Sinai, enclosed in a church of red and white granite entered from the west, five feet in length and four in depth; he notes that the Jewish writers hold it the cleft of the rock in which Moses was put, but refuses the identification on the text’s own showing, since if so there would have been no need for Elijah to go forth and stand upon the mount when the Lord passed by. He passes on the Targum’s reading of the three signs as hosts of angels of wind, of commotion and of fire, ministers going before the Lord to prepare the way of his glorious Majesty, and takes them as emblems of a power he could have displayed to the destruction of his enemies, and of the idolatrous kingdom of Israel, had he not chosen rather to use lenity and show mercy in what followed. On the wrapping of the face he reads reverence of the divine Majesty together with shame and confusion under a sense of impurity and unworthiness, and explains that Elijah had attempted to come forth at the divine order but was stopped a little within the cave by the terrible appearances, coming quite out only now to hear what the Lord would say.

Clarke leaves the question open, asking only whether it is a reproach for having fled from the face of Jezebel through what some call unbelieving fears, and conjectures with others that the cave is the same in which God put Moses. He lays out the complaint as four numbered charges against the nation, that they have forsaken the covenant and cleaved to other gods, endeavoured to abolish the worship and destroy its remembrance, slain the prophets so that none might reprove their iniquity or teach the truth, and determined not to rest until they had slain Elijah too. On the theophany he observes that Elijah was treated nearly as Moses had been and perhaps stood in the same place, that the passing by occasioned the wind, earthquake and fire, and that in none of these was God to make a discovery of himself, though they prepared the prophet to hear the still small voice; he reads the apparatus as a figure of law and gospel, the terrors serving only to introduce the mild spirit that proclaims peace and good will to men. He then reports fairly the alternative that all this was merely natural, the disturbed atmosphere, the agitation of the earth, the escaping fire and the returning gentle breeze describing a real earthquake in its ordinary order, but concludes that what took place was out of the ordinary course of nature and that the exciting cause of the whole was supernatural, quoting the Chaldee at length for the hosts of angels and for the voice as a singing in silence, a sound with which no other sound was mingled.

Alone in setting the vision against both earlier Horeb manifestations, to the people and to Moses, and in reading the night vision through the Greek insertion of to-morrow.
Alone in noticing that Moses was put into the cave when the glory passed while Elijah was called out of it, and alone in excusing the separate altars of the prophets as a schism God owned.

15.pericope_label: The commission to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha, and the seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal

schools.summary: Ellicott finds in the charge an indirect double rebuke: the cry that he was not better than his fathers, which implied that he stood out beyond all others to meet the stern requirements of the time, is met by the charge to delegate the task of vengeance for God to others; and the complaint that he alone was left is met by the revelation of the faithful remnant, the seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal, unknown to him and perhaps to one another but known and loved by God. He turns the incomplete fulfilment into evidence, since Elijah performed in person only the call of Elisha, this apparently imperfect correspondence of the event to the charge being a strong indication of the historical character of the narrative; he adds that no actual anointing of Elisha is recorded and that in no other place is the anointing of a prophet referred to, the rite having been instituted for the priests, extended next to the royal office and commonly attached to it, and though the prophetic office might well be hallowed by the same ordinance, especially as the prophets dispensed it to the kings, whether they were always consecrated with the sacred oil, or whether, as in the Prophet of prophets, the anointing with the Holy Ghost and with power sometimes superseded the outward sign, he says we do not know. Of Abelmeholah he notes that the name means the meadow of the dance and that it lay in the rich country near the Jordan valley and the plain of Esdraelon, and so on Elijah’s way. On the sword given to Elisha he grants the mission was plainly not one of vengeance, since he had to destroy enmity but not to slay the enemies of God, and makes the difficulty another mark of historic accuracy: the mission is probably described in the terms in which Elijah would best understand it, for his spirit was for war and he could hardly have conceived how its completion was to be wrought out by the weapons of peace in the hand of his successor. On the remnant he would render the words I leave, or will leave, through all this vengeance, and sets the seven thousand beside the faithful sealed in the visions of Ezekiel and of the Revelation in the day of God’s judgment; of the kissing he says the passage vividly describes the worshipper bowing the knee on first approach and on nearer access kissing the image, or the altar, or the threshold of the temple.

Gill has the prophet bidden back the way he came, through the wilderness of Arabia, which was part of his road to Damascus, near which was another wilderness taking its name from the city; but he passes on the suggestion of Fortunatus Schacchus that the phrase means no other than a return to his former course and custom of preaching the law of God and reclaiming men from the error of their ways. He observes that Jehu was in fact anointed not by Elijah but by Elisha, and that being done by his order and direction it was the same as if Elijah had done it himself, unless the man was anointed twice; that Jehu was a son of Jehoshaphat and a grandson of Nimshi; and that the double sword suggests many should be slain in Israel by Hazael and Jehu both. Of the seven thousand he notes only that they were left from perishing by the sword of either of them.

Clarke observes that the road given him is not one on which he would be likely to meet Jezebel or any other of his enemies, and explains the purpose of these revolutions from the verse that follows: God was about to bring his judgments upon the land and especially on the house of Ahab, exterminating it by Jehu, who was himself a scourge to the people, while Hazael grievously afflicted Israel. He denies that Elisha ever used the sword or commissioned it to be used, though he delivered solemn prophecies against a disobedient people, and settles the matter by chronology, since Elisha was prophet before Hazael was king and Hazael king before Jehu, and the famine he brought on the land preceded both reigns: the order of time here is not to be regarded, and the meaning is that the three shall be ministers of vengeance. He takes the seven thousand for many thousands, seven being a number of perfection as in the barren who has borne seven and gold seven times purified, and suspects that while the court and the multitudes had gone after Baal the majority of the common people still worshipped in secret the God of their fathers. On the kissing he traces adoration itself to the gesture, the word compounded of the Latin for to and for mouth, and gathers his witnesses: Pliny, that in the act of adoration we kiss the right hand and turn the whole body about; Cicero, on a statue of Hercules whose chin and lips were worn by the frequent kissing of worshippers; and his own observation of old paintings of the saints whose lips and mouths had been literally worn away by devotees. He also reports and rejects a rabbinic turn on the appointment of Elisha, that Elijah’s prophetic office displeased God because he was the constant accuser of his children.

The two swords suggest how many in Israel should be slain by Hazael and Jehu both

19.pericope_label: Elijah finds Elisha at the plough, casts his mantle upon him, and Elisha makes a farewell feast and follows

schools.summary: Henry presses where the man was found: not in the schools of the prophets but in the field, not reading nor praying nor sacrificing but ploughing, and though a great man, master of the ground and the oxen and the servants, he thought it no disparagement to follow his business himself and lay his own hand to the plough — idleness is no man’s honour, nor is husbandry any man’s disgrace, and an honest calling in the world does not put us out of the way of our heavenly calling, Elisha being taken from the plough to feed Israel as the apostles were taken from fishing to catch men. He notes that Elisha enquired not after Elijah but was anticipated with the call, as we choose God because he chose us first, and that Elijah was far from jealous of his successor but rejoiced to leave the work in such good hands. He reads the mantle as a token of friendship, Elijah taking him under his care as under his mantle, or of his being clothed with his master’s spirit as Moses put his honour upon Joshua, observing that at the ascent the mantle came to him entire. He distinguishes the request to take leave from the hesitation rebuked in the gospel: this was not an excuse for delay, like the man’s who desired to bid farewell to those at home, but only a reservation of the respect and duty owed to a father and mother. And he finds in the reply a care for the will, Elijah refusing to force him or take him against his will, letting him sit down and count the cost and make it his own act, since the efficacy of God’s grace preserves the native liberty of man’s will, so that those who are good are good of choice and not by constraint, not pressed men but volunteers. The feast proves the call acceptable, though he quit the comforts of his father’s house and expose himself to Jezebel’s party at a discouraging time for prophets to set out in, when a man who had consulted with flesh and blood would not have been fond of Elijah’s mantle; and from the ministry that followed he draws that those who would be fit to teach must have time to learn, and those who hope to rise and rule must be willing first to stoop and serve.

Clarke reckons the cost: twelve yoke of oxen imply a considerable estate, so that in obeying the prophetic call Elisha did it at considerable secular loss, and he notes that every owner of an inheritance among the Hebrews, and among the ancients generally, was a principal agent in its cultivation. He allows that the mantle may mark either a call to the prophetic office or an indication that he was called to be the prophet’s servant, the garment being the peculiar habit of a prophet and probably made of skin dressed with the hair on. He reads the reply as a disclaimer of agency — thy call is not from me but from God, and to him, not to me, art thou accountable for thy use or abuse of it — and observes that Elisha conferred not with flesh and blood but resolved immediately to obey, wishing only to bid his relatives farewell. He takes the boiling of the flesh with the agricultural implements for a token that he had abandoned secular life; and he draws two lessons, that a call to the ministry, though it sever a man completely from secular occupation, never supersedes the duties of filial affection, and that the parents made no attempt to hinder him, having too much respect for the authority of God. He ventures furthest in conjecturing that the popes borrowed from this act the ceremony of investing an archbishop with the pall, retailing from Durandus how the lambs offered by the nuns of Agnes were shorn, how the wool was woven and the pall laid on the high altar over the bodies of the apostles and carried away after a vigil, and how, being taken from the body of the apostle, it was held to signify the plenitude of ecclesiastical power; he notes too that the Greek philosophers wore a mantle distinguishing them from common people as gowns and square caps distinguish certain academic ranks, and reads the warning in Zechariah as aimed at those who took the prophetic dress without the prophetic call.

Keil and Delitzsch put the sign plainly: the prophet’s cloak was the sign of the prophet’s vocation, so that throwing it to him as he passed was a symbol of the call to the prophetic office, and the twelve yoke before him with himself at the twelfth mark a very wealthy man. They read the reply as permission with a disclaimer, the words meaning that Elijah had not wanted to put any constraint upon him, and set the two fields side by side: as he had ploughed his earthly field with his twelve pair of oxen, he was now to plough the spiritual field of the twelve tribes of Israel. Of the feast they give the plain sequence, that he took the pair with which he had been ploughing and slaughtered them, boiled the flesh with the plough, gave a farewell meal to the people of his place of abode, that is his friends and acquaintance, and then followed Elijah as his servant and assistant. Ellicott renders the twelve yoke, or as Ewald has it of land, as indicating wealth in the family which he had to leave to follow a wandering life, and marks the contrast between the two prophets in the difference of their home and origin, the quiet simplicity of this call standing against the sudden and mysterious appearance of Elijah. He describes the garment as the rough hair-mantle characteristic of the ascetic recluse and reports that the act is said to have been part of the form of adopting a child, which would give its spiritual significance here, read by Elisha after a moment’s bewilderment. On the request he finds it impossible not to compare the similar one made to our Lord by a man who declared himself ready to follow, and hears in Elijah’s answer a half-ironical rebuke of what seemed hesitation — go back, if thou wilt; what have I done to constrain thee? — both cases showing the stern but necessary rejection of half-hearted service even where the heart is distracted by the most natural and sacred love, though he grants that Elijah saw the man meant simply farewell and apparently waited till it was over. Of the feast he says that, like Matthew, Elisha makes a meal of farewell to his home and of homage to his new master, the wooden implements serving for hasty fuel as at the threshing-floor of Araunah, and notes what he accepted: henceforth from a master he became a servant, willing to be known, even when he was himself the prophet of God, as he that poured water on the hands of Elijah.

Gill measures the journey, Bunting computing Abelmeholah at a hundred and fifty-six miles from Horeb; he explains that Elisha left the oxen and ran because his heart was touched by the Lord at the same time and his mind enlightened to understand what was meant by that action; and he has him return to his father’s house to take his leave and then come back into the field, perhaps with others accompanying him.
